papers.title: Towards the Query Complexity of Sampling under Strong Log-Concavity and Log-Sobolev Inequalities
papers.abstract: We study the query complexity of sampling from smooth distributions on $\mathbb R^d$ using first-order oracles. For $d$-dimensional strongly log-concave targets with condition number $\kappa=2$, we prove that any randomized sampler requires $\exp({\Omega(\log^{1/3} d)})$ queries even from a constant warm start. This rules out polylogarithmic dimension dependence and strictly separates strongly log-concave sampling from Gaussian sampling. For targets with $L$-smooth potentials satisfying an $\alpha$-log-Sobolev inequality with $\kappa= L/\alpha$, we prove an $\Omega(\kappa)$ query lower bound for $d\gtrsim\log^2\kappa$. This shows that log-Sobolev sampling is strictly harder than strongly log-concave sampling. Our proofs construct instance-dependent tests that target samples typically pass but outputs of algorithms making few queries typically fail. For strongly log-concave targets, we embed a sequence of hidden Gaussian into high-degree tensor polynomial with smooth gates, forcing any algorithm to uncover the layers sequentially. The log-Sobolev construction hides a constant fraction of the target mass in angular caps while controlling the log-Sobolev constant via delicate estimates.

papers.title: Improved lower bounds on the approximability of Multiway Cut using Sherali-Adams relaxations
papers.abstract: The Multiway Cut problem is among the most well-studied problems in the area of combinatorial approximation algorithms. The currently best approximation ratio for the problem is 1.2787, obtained recently by the authors (2026). The best lower bound on the approximation ratio that can be achieved for the problem in polynomial time, under the Unique Games Conjecture (UGC), is 1.20016, obtained by B\'erczi, Chandrasekaran, Kir\'aly, and Madan (2020), building on and slightly improving a bound of $\frac65=1.2$, obtained by Angelidakis, Makarychev, and Manurangsi (2017) by introducing the important framework of non-opposite multiway cuts. We obtain a substantially improved lower bound of 1.22232 on the approximation ratio of the Multiway Cut problem. Manokaran, Naor, Raghavendra, and Schwartz (2008) showed that under UGC, the approximation ratio of Multiway Cut is equal to the integrality ratio of a simple LP relaxation, known as the CKR relaxation, introduced by C\u{a}linescu, Karloff, and Rabani (2000). Thus, stronger LP relaxations are not required for obtaining an optimal approximation algorithm for the problem. We show, however, that relying on the framework of Angelidakis, Makarychev, and Manurangsi (2017), stronger LP relaxations from the Sherali-Adams hierarchy for non-opposite multiway cuts can be used to obtain improved integrality ratios for the CKR relaxation, and hence improved lower bounds on the approximation ratio of the Multiway Cut problem. One of the novel features of our analysis is considering a continuous limit of discrete LPs defined on a simplex. Our proof of the new 1.22232 bound is completely analytic. We also present strong numerical evidence that suggests that our techniques can be used to improve the lower bound to at least 1.23003.

papers.title: Do Language Models Know Which Constraints Belong Together?
papers.abstract: Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation strengthens the linear relaxation of a mixed-integer program by convexifying a chosen set of constraint families, and every candidate costs a column generation run. The choice is hard when families strengthen the bound only together, because a search that adds one family at a time then stops at the linear relaxation. The classical inequalities of lot sizing, network design and facility location rest on such zero-marginal groups. We prove that when each evaluation convexifies at most $s$ of $k$ families, any method that observes only bounds needs a covering number of evaluations, of order $k^w$, to find a hidden group of $w$ families, also on actual Dantzig-Wolfe relaxations. A prediction that misses $e$ members reduces the cost to $\Theta(k^e)$, through one staged search that does not need to know $e$, so the evaluations a prediction saves measure what the predictor knows. We study two sources of predictions. A one-pass lookahead at an optimal LP dual is provably blind to groups whose families share no variable, and a language model reads the names and text of the model. JointDW verifies the prediction of the language model with the staged search and interleaves it with the lookahead at a bounded loss. Groups that strengthen the bound only jointly appear in a quarter of the MIPLIB-NL models whose bound can be improved. There the strongest language models identify them about as often as the lookahead, their predictions rest on the names for textbook models, and reasoning about doubles the accuracy of the same model. On larger models with distracting families, the lookahead finds the group in one evaluation of three families. Language models given only the text seldom name it, while one reasoning model given every coefficient names it in all but one answer and then needs fewer evaluations than the lookahead for pairs of families.

papers.title: Softmax Attention with Any Temperature in Fixed Dimension: Matching the Best Known Maximum-Inner-Product Bounds
authors: Zixuan Huang (State Key Laboratory of Multimedia Information Processing
Guozhang Chen (State Key Laboratory of Multimedia Information Processing
National Engineering Research Center of Visual Technology
papers.abstract: Attention is central to modern AI models for language, vision, and scientific modeling. However, direct evaluation compares every query with every key, requiring quadratic time in the context length, which limits its scalability to long contexts. Consequently, characterizing the complexity bounds of attention is of fundamental importance. For every fixed dimension $d$, we give an algorithm for $m$ queries, $n$ key-value pairs, and additive error $\varepsilon$, with expected time $ \widetilde{\mathrm{O}}\bigl((mn)^{k/(k+1)}+m+n\bigr),\qquad k=\lfloor d/2\rfloor. $ For fixed dimension and a fixed number of value channels, soft-O hides factors of the form $\operatorname{poly}_d\bigl(b,\log(m+n),\log B,\log(1/\varepsilon)\bigr),$ where $b$ bounds input encoding lengths and $B$ bounds coordinate and value magnitudes. In particular, the dependence on $B$ and $1/\varepsilon$ is polylogarithmic, which allows arbitrary positive temperature. When $m=n$ and $d\ge2$, the bound is $\widetilde{\mathrm{O}}(n^{2-2/(\lfloor d/2\rfloor+1)})$: near-linear in dimensions two and three, with exponent $4/3$ in dimensions four and five and $3/2$ in dimensions six and seven. It improves the previous $\widetilde{\mathrm{O}}(n^{2-1/d})$ upper bound and matches the best known batch maximum-inner-product bound in each fixed dimension. Additionally, we reduce integer batch maximum inner product computation to one attention call with the same dimension and input sizes $m,n$.

papers.title: Constant-Round Massively Parallel Algorithms for Approximate MSTs in Metric Spaces
papers.abstract: We develop a unified algorithmic framework for computing approximate minimum spanning trees (MSTs) in metric spaces in the fully scalable Massively Parallel Computation (MPC) model. Using this framework, we obtain the following results for any fixed constant $\sigma\in(0,1)$: - General metrics: Given all pairwise distances, we compute a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate MST in $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ rounds using $n^\sigma$ local space per machine and $\widetilde{O}(n^2)$ total space. - Euclidean spaces: Given $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we compute an $O(1/\sigma^4)$-approximate MST in $O(1)$ rounds using $(nd)^\sigma$ local space per machine and $O(nd+n^{1+\sigma})$ total space. - Doubling metrics: Given $n$ points in a metric of doubling dimension $\mathrm{ddim}=O(\sigma\log n)$, we compute an $O(1/\sigma)$-approximate MST in $O(\mathrm{ddim}/\sigma^4)$ rounds using $n^\sigma$ local space per machine and $\widetilde{O}(n^{1+\sigma})\cdot 2^{O(\mathrm{ddim})}$ total space. For any fixed constant $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, these results give the first constant-round MPC algorithms achieving $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation in general metrics and $O(1)$-approximation in a high-dimensional Euclidean space, respectively. They improve upon the $O(\log\log n+\log(1/\varepsilon))$-round algorithm for general metrics [SODA'25] and the $O(\log\log n\cdot\log\log\log n)$-round algorithm for Euclidean spaces [SODA'24], respectively. Moreover, our round complexity for general metrics is asymptotically optimal in its dependence on $\varepsilon$, matching the $\Omega(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ lower bound of [SODA'25] under the 1-vs-2-cycles conjecture. Our result also answers an open question raised by [STOC'23].

papers.title: Query-Oblivious Coresets for Softmax Attention: Improved Bounds and Efficient Constructions
papers.abstract: A query-oblivious coreset for a softmax-attention head is a subset of the key--value pairs whose attention output is within $\varepsilon$ of the full one for every query in a ball. With $\rho$ the query radius times the centred key radius, we build such coresets of size $O(e^{\rho}(\sqrt{d_v}+\sqrt{d_k\log(1+\rho)})/\varepsilon)$ in randomised polynomial time, improving the existential $O(\sqrt d\,e^{\rho+\frac12\log\rho+o(\log\log\rho)}/\varepsilon)$ of Liberty, Andoni and Kleiner to within $\sqrt{\log(1+\rho)}$ of their $\Omega(\sqrt d\,e^{\rho}/\varepsilon)$ lower bound: a spherical lift of both balls into one exponential-kernel instance admits the Bozzai--Rothvoss chaining bound, and Chevet's inequality splits key from value dimension. A sampling cap $O(e^{2\rho}/\varepsilon^{2})$ completes the envelope, and in fixed dimension Tai's diameter-free bound removes the logarithm. A census of every head of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct finds $\rho\ge24.100$, so every whole-ball bound with a factor $e^{\rho}/\varepsilon$ prescribes a coreset larger than the cache: the algorithmic contribution is asymptotic on these models.

papers.title: Ranking and Unranking Permutations in Heap's Order
papers.abstract: Heap's algorithm is a permutation generation method with very low constant overhead. Its element-interchanging mechanism, however, prevents the standard factorial-base Lehmer code from being applied directly, and to our knowledge no explicit Rank/Unrank algorithm for the Heap order has been published. This paper describes the block structure of Heap's algorithm in terms of rearrangement operators: the net effect of a block-internal traversal is a tail-preserving operator and the block-boundary swap is a top-level swap operator, and together they yield a closed-form recurrence for the block transitions. On this basis a bottom-up Unrank algorithm and a top-down Rank algorithm are built from one and the same closed-form in-block mapping; both run in $O(n^3)$ time and $O(n)$ space and require no factorial-scale precomputed table. The supporting proofs use a synchronized strong induction on the dimension to establish the bijectivity of the trailing-element mapping, closed forms for the final arrangement and for the trailing sequence, the dichotomy of its cycle structure, and the reciprocity of Rank and Unrank. The Heap order is in fact the colex order of the mixed-radix code.

papers.title: A Fully Polynomial Approximation Algorithm for the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick Model
papers.abstract: Montanari's incremental approximate message passing (IAMP) algorithm [FOCS 2019; SIAM J. Comput., 2025] and the zero-temperature formulation of El Alaoui, Montanari and Sellke (AMS) [Ann. Probab., 2021] find a $(1-\varepsilon)$ approximation to the maximum Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) energy in $C(\varepsilon)N^2$ operations for fixed accuracy, with probability tending to one as $N\to\infty$, under their respective full-support and access-model assumptions. However, it was unknown whether this approximation could be achieved with work polynomial in both $N$ and $1/\varepsilon$, together with quantitative guarantees at finite dimension. Under the same assumptions as AMS, we introduce grouped IAMP with exact Gaussian query outputs (GEG-IAMP), which is the first SK approximation algorithm with total work polynomial in $N$ and $1/\varepsilon$ and a finite-size guarantee above a dimension threshold polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$ and $\log(1/\alpha)$. More precisely, for every $\alpha\in(0,1/2)$, it returns a $(1-\varepsilon)$ approximation with probability at least $1-\alpha$ whenever $N\ge \mathsf{K}\varepsilon^{-2}\log^2(e/\varepsilon)\log(\mathsf{K}/\alpha)$, using $O(N^2/\varepsilon)$ work and $O(N^2)$ storage. GEG-IAMP replaces the Onsager correction by Reeves's coupling construction [arXiv:2508.10782] and groups Euler-Maruyama steps into $O(1/\varepsilon)$ matrix-vector products. We also prove a relative guarantee for AMS IAMP with $O(N^2\varepsilon^{-3}\log^2(e/\varepsilon))$ work but a sufficient dimension exponential in inverse accuracy. By returning a fixed configuration below its dimension threshold, GEG-IAMP also provides an asymptotic fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme (AFPRAS), with an additive error independent of dimension.

papers.title: Fast Quantum Byzantine Agreement with Nearly Linear Quantum Communication
papers.abstract: We consider synchronous binary Byzantine agreement among $n$ processes connected by authenticated point-to-point classical and quantum channels. The adversary is computationally unbounded, sees all classical information, adaptively corrupts up to $t\le(1/3-\varepsilon)n$ processes, and may suppress messages sent by a process in the round in which it is corrupted. We give a quantum algorithm that solves Byzantine agreement in this model with probability $1$. It uses $O(\log^4 n)$ rounds, $O(n\log^8 n)$ qubits, and $O(n^2\log^8 n)$ classical bits in expectation, with constants depending on $\varepsilon$. This reduces the quantum communication of the protocol of Ben-Or and Hassidim (STOC~2005), which achieves $O(1)$ expected rounds but whose Byzantine coin implementation requires $\Omega(n^4\log n)$ qubits and classical bits. We also extend the quadratic message lower bound of Abraham et al.\ (PODC~2019) to quantum channels, obtaining an $\Omega(t^2)$ lower bound on worst-case expected total communication. For $t=\Theta(n)$, the communication and round complexity of our algorithm are therefore optimal up to polylogarithmic factors.

papers.title: Private Online Release of Adaptive Linear Queries
papers.abstract: In this paper we study answering counting and other linear queries online under differential privacy constraints. Recent work by Nikolov, Tang, and Ullman [STOC 2026] gave the first online algorithm that answers \emph{obliviously chosen} online linear queries privately, and achieves poly-logarithmic competitiveness against an optimal offline factorization mechanism. This also implied poly-logarithmic competitiveness against arbitrary private offline mechanisms when the private dataset is large enough. The error guarantees of their algorithm, however, can fail when the queries are adaptive. We give a new algorithm that also achieves poly-logarithmic competitiveness, while being able to handle \emph{adaptively chosen} queries. This implies that there is no large separation between the optimal error bounds for privately answering, respectively, offline linear queries, obliviously chosen online linear queries, and adaptively chosen online linear queries. Our algorithm combines the online factorization approach from prior work with a novel layered Euclidean iterative database construction, presenting a new way to use factorization in private algorithms. We also give a lower bound that shows that some poly-logarithmic factor in the competitive ratio is unavoidable. Our lower bound first shows that any interactive private mechanism implies a deterministic online factorization algorithm, and then gives a new lower bound for the competitive ratio of any deterministic online factorization algorithm.

papers.title: The Harmonic Online $k$-Server Algorithm Is Poly(k)-Competitive
papers.abstract: The online $k$-server problem is one of the most fundamental problems in online algorithms. In this problem, $k$ servers are located in a metric space and serve a sequence of requests at points in the metric space by moving a server there. The Harmonic algorithm is a very natural algorithm: it chooses a server with probability inversely proportional to its distance from the request. It is also highly efficient, being memoryless and answering each request in $O(k)$ time. However, its competitive ratio has remained unsettled between the $O(2^k \log k)$ upper bound (Bartal and Grove, JACM 2000) and the $k(k+1)/2$ lower bound (Raghavan and Snir, 1994, IBM J. Res. Dev.). We prove that Harmonic is $2k^4$-competitive on every metric space against adaptive online adversaries. Our analysis uses a potential combining corrected electrical energy with the distances of online servers to their assigned adversary locations.

papers.title: Reachability Diameter: Beyond the Square-Root Barrier, with Polynomial Hardness
papers.abstract: The reachability diameter of a directed graph is the maximum finite shortest-path distance across all pairs of vertices. It has received recent attention under this name, although the underlying quantity has long played a central role in shortcut set and parallel reachability. Notably, Bals et al. establish hardness for every polynomial-factor approximation in nearly-linear time for weighted digraphs. Yet they give $n^{1/2+o(1)}$-approximation in the unweighted regime with nearly-linear running time, and their conditional lower bounds rule out certain constants only, leaving open whether polynomial loss is necessary. We give a randomized algorithm that estimates the reachability diameter of an unweighted digraph within a factor $n^{1/3+o(1)}$, with high probability, in $\widetilde{O}(m+n)$ time. We complement our algorithm with a lower bound conditional on the 3-uniform Hyperclique hypothesis, ruling out an $n^{2/15-\varepsilon}$-approximation in $\widetilde{O}(m+n)$ time for every fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,2/15)$, establishing the necessity of polynomial loss for nearly-linear time algorithms.

papers.title: Incremental Minimum Spanning Trees on a Napkin
papers.abstract: In the incremental minimum spanning forest problem, weighted edges arrive one at a time. After each insertion we must report the edge that leaves the minimum spanning forest, and queries ask for the bottleneck distance of two vertices: the smallest possible maximum edge cost on a path between them. Link-cut trees solve both in $O(\log n)$ amortized time. In 2021 we wrote the folklore BottleneckTree, a short competitive-programming structure that stores one parent pointer and one cost per vertex, and conjectured that it also runs in $O(\log n)$ amortized time. We show that this conjecture is false: on a family of inputs, its amortized cost per operation is $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$. We then present a structure with the same state, two arrays and a single loop, and prove that it runs in $O(\log n)$ amortized time per insertion and per query. Unlike the AM-tree of Ding, Gu and Sun, which attains the same bound, it stores no subtree sizes and maintains no balance invariant. For a connected graph with distinct costs, the structure can be viewed as an implicit link-cut tree on the Kruskal reconstruction tree: each rotation corresponds to exactly one preferred-child change, and each skip acts on a stale path-parent pointer. In experiments it is 1.3-2.1 times faster than the folklore BottleneckTree on insertions, up to 480 times faster on its adversarial input, and 6.3-16 times faster than an explicit link-cut tree.

papers.title: Faster Approximate Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances via Near-Optimal Sumset Estimation
papers.abstract: \emph{Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances} is one of the most studied problems in string algorithms: given a text $T$ of length~$n$ and a pattern~$P$, the task is to compute the Hamming distance between~$P$ and every length-$|P|$ substring of~$T$. As exact algorithms have been stuck at time~$\tilde O(n^{3/2})$ for decades, a long line of work has turned to the $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate version of the problem. Milestones include Karloff's $\tilde O(\epsilon^{-2} n)$-time algorithm [IPL '93], followed by randomized improvements to $\tilde O(\epsilon^{-1} n)$ by Kopelowitz and Porat [FOCS '15] and recently to $\tilde O(\epsilon^{-0.915} n)$ by Chan, Jin, Vassilevska W., and Xu [FOCS '23]. In this work, we significantly improve this bound to $\tilde O(\epsilon^{-2/3} n)$, using a considerably simpler algorithm. Our algorithm follows the framework of Chan, Jin, Vassilevska W., and Xu, which reduces the problem to a variant of 3SUM that we call \emph{Sumset Estimation}. We solve Sumset Estimation optimally (up to logarithmic factors) by replacing their matrix multiplication techniques with ideas from sparse recovery. Specifically, we adapt the classic Count Sketch by replacing its random signs with random complex roots of unity---a simple idea that may find further applications for other additive problems. Finally, we give evidence that our running time might in fact be optimal: we show that the $\epsilon^{-2/3}$ dependence is \emph{best possible} for a certain natural class of algorithms, including ours and all previous algorithms.

papers.title: Flow-Optimal Separators for Minor-Free and Induced-Minor-Free Graphs in Linear Time via Follow the Regularized Leader
papers.abstract: We give a new algorithm for finding balanced separators in minor-free and induced-minor-free graphs. A key technical idea is a new connection to online learning: we formulate a continuous, non-convex optimization problem and solve it using the Follow the Regularized Leader (FTRL) framework. Our implementation of each FTRL step yields a purely combinatorial algorithm that assigns and adjusts vertex weights over multiple rounds. For graphs with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, we obtain the following results. (1) For $H$-induced-minor-free graphs, we find a balanced separator of size $O(\log(|V(H)|)\sqrt{|V(H)|+|E(H)|}\sqrt{m})$ in expected linear time for fixed $H$. As a corollary, we find balanced separators of size $O(\sqrt{m})$ in string graphs in expected linear time, without requiring string representations. (2) For $K_h$-minor-free graphs, we find a balanced separator of size $O(h\log h\sqrt{n})$ in expected linear time for fixed $h$. Our algorithm unifies two long lines of work on separators in minor-free graphs, dating back to Alon, Seymour, and Thomas (1990): one optimizing separator size and the other optimizing running time. It also gives a natural interpretation of the vertex weighting scheme in a recent linear-time algorithm by Bonnet, Korhonen, Le, Li, and Masarik (2026). The separator bounds for both graph classes are flow-optimal: techniques based on flow-cut duality, including ours, cannot yield balanced separators of asymptotically smaller size.

papers.title: Noncrossing is All You Need: Beyond Identical Delay Functions in Online Matching with Delays on General Metrics
papers.abstract: Online optimization with delays has emerged as a powerful paradigm with numerous applica- tions, including matching, caching, server management, network design, and set cover. In most of these problems, competitive algorithms are known for arbitrary monotone delay functions, even when different requests are associated with different delay functions. The notable exception is online matching with delays, where all previously known algorithms achieving constant or polylogarithmic competitive ratios require the delay functions to be identical, either linear or concave, and known in advance. We study the online minimum-cost perfect matching with delays problem on general metrics. We introduce the broad class of noncrossing delay functions, which strictly generalizes the classic setting of identical concave delay functions while naturally modeling scenarios in which different requests may experience different delay costs. We present the first deterministic $O(1)$-competitive algorithm for the single-location online matching problem with noncrossing delay functions in the non-clairvoyant setting as well as a randomized $O(lognlog\Delta+log^2\Delta)$-competitive algorithm of an arbitrary metric space where $n$ is the number of points of the metric space and $\Delta$ is its aspect ratio. Our result allows each request to have an arbitrary noncrossing delay function, thereby simultaneously removing the assumptions of identical delay functions, concavity, and clairvoyance that were required by all previous constant or polylogarithmic-competitive algorithms.

papers.title: Sublinear Metric Distortion for Matching
papers.abstract: We study metric distortion in one-sided matching. Given $n$ agents and $n$ items in an unknown metric space, our goal is to match agents to items so that the total distance between matched pairs is small. However, instead of direct access to the distances in the metric, we are only given each agent's ranking of the items by distance. What is the smallest worst-case approximation factor (called the distortion) that a mechanism can guarantee in expectation? Despite significant interest over the last decade, the best-known guarantee has been the $O(n)$ distortion of Random Serial Dictatorship since the beginning. We give a matching mechanism with distortion $O(n^{\log_4 3})$, the first sublinear upper bound. The key idea is to use a partial matching derived from a truncated version of either Random Serial Dictatorship or the Probabilistic Serial rule. We then complete this matching using a new, general-purpose cluster completion algorithm that ensures unmatched agents receive nearby items. Along the way, we pin down the optimal distortion of Random Serial Dictatorship and Probabilistic Serial up to logarithmic and constant factors, respectively, and give improved lower bounds for truthful mechanisms.

papers.title: Makespan Bounds for Synchronous Pebble Motion on Graphs
papers.abstract: We study the largest minimum makespan of labeled pebble motion on graphs under a model that permits synchronous pebble movement. While classical pebble motion on graphs allows only one pebble to move at a time, our model permits any number of pebbles to move to an adjacent vertex, provided that no two pebbles collide. At full occupancy every vertex is assigned a pebble and a legal round consists of disjoint cycle rotations. We prove a series of makespan bounds for this problem on graphs with varying structure and pebble density. For cycles with a chord, we extend a known quadratic bound at span two to every fixed span. For random cubic graphs, we convert permutation routing via matchings into legal schedules in two ways, applying cycle-cover batching at full occupancy and disjoint vacancy-delivery paths below full occupancy. For simple 3-connected planar cubic graphs, we prove a tight linear class maximum at every pebble count. We extend the results to increasing degree, common-neighbor conditions, and vertex connectivity. The results describe how graph connectivity, cycle structure, expansion, planarity, and occupancy affect worst-case routing time.

papers.title: Improved Bounds on Distance Preservers
papers.abstract: Given an undirected unweighted graph $G$ on $n$ vertices and a set $P$ of $p$ pairs of its vertices, a distance preserver is a sparse subgraph of $G$ that exactly preserves the shortest-path distances between all pairs in $P$. In this paper, we prove a new upper bound of $O(n^{8/9} p^{4/9})$ for distance preservers when $p\in [n^{1/2}, n]$. Our result improves the previous bound of $O\big(n^{2/3}p^{2/3}+np^{1/3}\big)$ by Bodwin and Vassilevska Williams and $O(\min\{n+n^{1/2}p,\,np^{1/2}\})$ by Coppersmith and Elkin, particularly in the regime $p\in [n^{7/10}, n]$, and narrows the gap toward the conjectured $O(n^{2/3}p^{2/3}+n)$ bound. Using the techniques developed for distance preservers, we are also able to obtain pairwise additive $+2$ spanners with $O(n+n^{9/10}p^{2/5})$ edges, pairwise additive $+4$ spanners with $O(n+n^{24/25}p^{8/25})$ edges, and new bounds for sourcewise spanners, improving upon previous results in certain parameter regimes.

papers.title: Improved approximation algorithms for capacitated cluster editing
papers.abstract: We study the minimum-disagreement cluster editing problem that, from a complete edge-signed graph, where a positive edge represents two vertices agreeing to each other while a negative represents a disagreement, constructs disjoint cliques of upper bounded size such that the total number of negative edges inside cliques and positive edges outside cliques is minimized. When the sizes of the candidate cliques are unbounded, the problem is NP-hard and APX-hard, and many approximation algorithms with improving ratios have been proposed in the literature and the state-of-the-art approximation ratio of $\alpha = 1.3865 + \epsilon$. The capacitated variant, in which the candidate cliques have sizes no greater than a given $k$, is less studied and the best approximation ratio is $5.37$. In this paper, we study the latter problem. We first present a downsizing procedure that achieves an approximation ratio of $\alpha_k = 2 \alpha + 1$, based on any $\alpha$-approximation algorithm for the uncapacitated problem. Secondly, we propose a hybrid of cluster-LP sampling and pivoting and show that for every fractional capacitated cluster-LP solution of cost $L$, the hybrid using ordinary pivoting has an expected cost at most $\frac 95 L + \frac 1{10} \OPT_k$, and the hybrid using conditional pivoting has an expected cost at most $\frac {306}{203} L + \frac {50}{203} \OPT_k$. A cardinality-constrained adaptation of the approximate dual-separation framework of Garc\'ia-Soriano and Schohn supplies the required fractional solution and yields a randomized $(1.9 + \epsilon)$-approximation algorithm and a randomized $(1.7537 + \epsilon)$-approximation algorithm, respectively.

papers.title: Faster Isomorphism for Groups of Class 2
papers.abstract: The finite-group isomorphism problem asks whether two groups, given by their Cayley tables, are isomorphic. Despite decades of study, obtaining an $N^{o(\log N)}$-time algorithm for general groups of order $N$ remains a major open challenge. Groups of nilpotency class $2$ have long been a central obstacle to achieving this goal. Recent breakthroughs have established $N^{o(\log N)}$-time algorithms for $p$-groups of class $2$ with odd $p$ (Sun, STOC '23; Ivanyos-Mendoza-Qiao-Sun-Zhang, FOCS '24; Grochow-Qiao-Stange-Sun, STOC '25) and for groups of Frattini class $2$ (Grochow-Ivanyos-Qiao-Sun, FOCS '26). However, the problem remained open for general groups of class $2$. In this paper, we present an algorithm for testing isomorphism of groups of class $2$, with running time $N^{O((\log N)^{25/26} \log \log N)}$. Our algorithm combines a tensor-based restriction of the search space, an encoding of group relations by alternating matrix tuples, and an orbit computation to recover the remaining central power information.

papers.title: Faster Dynamic Maximal Independent Set against Adaptive Adversaries
papers.abstract: We study the fully dynamic maximal independent set (MIS) problem: maintaining an MIS in an undirected graph on $n$ vertices with at most $m$ edges under edge insertions and deletions. Against an oblivious adversary, which fixes the edge update sequence in advance, the randomized algorithms of Behnezhad et al. (2019) and Chechik and Zhang (2019) achieve polylogarithmic update time. Against an adaptive adversary, which may choose each update after observing the previously reported MISs, the best previously known update bound was $O(m^{2/3})$, given by the deterministic algorithm of Gupta and Khan (2018, 2021). Assuming the combinatorial Boolean matrix multiplication hypothesis, Bernstein et al. (2026) proved that any combinatorial algorithm against an adaptive adversary requires at least $m^{1/2-o(1)}$ update time even under edge insertions alone, leaving a polynomial gap between upper and lower bounds. We present a randomized fully dynamic MIS algorithm with $\widetilde O(m^{5/8})=\widetilde O(m^{2/3-1/24})$ update time against adaptive adversaries. This gives the first polynomial improvement over the $m^{2/3}$ bound for adaptive fully dynamic MIS.

papers.title: Single-Variable Connectivity in Random $k$-SAT
papers.abstract: We resolve longstanding questions about connectivity, reconstruction,and looseness in random $k$-SAT, for sufficiently large fixed $k$ as the number $n$ of variables tends to infinity. $\textbf{Single-variable connectivity up to reconstruction.}$ At clause densities up to \[\frac{2^k}{k}\bigl(\ln k+\ln\ln k+\gamma_*-o_k(1)\bigr),\] a polynomial-time algorithm joins a typical pair of satisfying assignments with high probability, using $O_k(n)$ single-variable flips that preserve satisfiability. Here $\gamma_*\approx0.871$ arises from a refined tree-reconstruction analysis. $\textbf{Settling the reconstruction threshold.}$ Building on the tools developed for connectivity, we determine the clustering threshold defined by the reconstruction criterion to be \[\frac{2^k}{k}\bigl(\ln k+\ln\ln k+\gamma_*+o_k(1)\bigr),\] below the classical cavity prediction with constant term $1+O(\ln\ln k/\ln k)$. $\textbf{Shattering before rigidity.}$ We locate the looseness--rigidity transition at a higher density, matching the classical cavity prediction for clustering: \[\frac{2^k}{k} \left(\ln k+\ln\ln k+1+\Theta\left(\frac{\ln\ln k}{\ln k}\right)\right).\] Below the transition, we establish a stronger form of looseness: any variable of a typical solution can be reversed by logarithmically many single-variable flips that preserve satisfiability. Above it, reversing most variables of a typical solution requires changing linearly many variables (rigidity). Yet throughout an interval between reconstruction and rigidity, the solution space already splits into groups of exponentially small relative size separated by linear Hamming distance and linear energy barriers (shattering), while logarithmic looseness persists.

papers.title: Single-Exponential FPT Algorithms for Minimum Bisection and Matching Cut via a New Unbreakable Decomposition
papers.abstract: Minimum Bisection asks whether the vertices of a graph can be partitioned into two parts whose sizes differ by at most one and with at most k edges between the two parts. Cygan, Lokshtanov, Marcin Pilipczuk, Micha{\l} Pilipczuk, and Saurabh (SICOMP 2019) gave the first fixed-parameter algorithm, which runs in O*(2^(O(k^3))) time, by introducing an unbreakable decomposition. Cygan, Komosa, Lokshtanov, Marcin Pilipczuk, Micha{\l} Pilipczuk, Saurabh, and Wahlstr\"om (TALG 2021) strengthened the decomposition and improved the running time to O*(2^(O(k log k))). However, whether the running time could be improved to single-exponential remained open. In this paper, we give a deterministic O*(2^(O(k)))-time algorithm for Minimum Bisection. Our algorithm also counts all feasible bisections. To obtain an O*(2^(O(k)))-time algorithm, we introduce two new techniques. First, we give a new algorithm that computes a (2k,k)-edge-unbreakable decomposition with adhesion at most 2k in O*(2^(O(k))) time by relaxing the unbreakability and adhesion guarantees of the decomposition in (TALG 2021). Second, we improve the running time of the dynamic program over the decomposition from O*(2^(O(k log k))) to O*(2^(O(k))) using important cuts, inclusion-exclusion, and formal logarithms and exponentials. Together with color coding, the same techniques give a deterministic O*(2^(O(k)))-time algorithm for Matching Cut, which asks for a cut whose crossing edges form a matching. This improves the O*(2^(O(k log k)))-time algorithm of Aravind and Saxena (IWOCA 2021).

papers.title: Faster Cluster Decomposition with Stronger Bi-Criteria Guarantee
papers.abstract: Partitioning the vertex set of a graph $G=(V,E)$ into clusters is a classical problem in computer science. As vertices within clusters should be well connected and cuts between clusters sparse, Oveis Gharan and Trevisan (SODA 2014, [OGT14]) proposed to measure the partition quality using inner and outer conductance, i.e., the bi-criteria guarantee. Specifically, when partitioning $V$ into vertex-disjoint subsets $P_1,\ldots, P_k$, every subgraph induced by $P_i$ should have high conductance, while the conductance of $P_i$ in $G$ should be low. They studied the existence of such a partition and designed a polynomial-time algorithm achieving this guarantee. For more than a decade, their algorithm remained the only one achieving this guarantee on its output clusters. In this paper, we study faster cluster decomposition algorithms under the same setup as [OGT14] and prove three results: 1. We make their existential result algorithmic: Our algorithms run in nearly-linear time, and achieve the same bi-criteria guarantee as the one in [OGT14] up to constant factors, including the asymptotically tight dependence on $k$. 2. We prove that their existential result holds algorithmically under a much weaker condition on the initial disjoint subsets. To achieve this, we develop a general algorithm framework that boosts the approximation guarantee of a solution: given an $\alpha$-approximate solution to the $k$-way conductance problem, if $\rho_G(k+1)/\rho_G(k)=\Omega\left(\alpha/\varepsilon\right)$, then a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate solution can be obtained using only $O(k(1+\log\alpha))$ minimum $s$-$t$ cut computations. 3. We present a nearly-linear time algorithm that finds clusters with the bi-criteria guarantee. Our algorithm has the same guarantee as the one in [OGT14], which, for any unweighted graph of $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, runs in $\widetilde{O}(knm^2)$ time.

papers.title: Optimal LCA and Sublinear Estimation for Bipartite Matching in $\Delta^{O(1/\varepsilon)}$ Queries
papers.abstract: A local computation algorithm (LCA) for matching answers ``who is the mate of $v$?'' by inspecting only a small part of the graph, with all answers consistent with one matching. For $n$-vertex graphs of maximum degree $\Delta\ge2$, Levi et al. [Algorithmica'17] give a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximate matching LCA using $(\Delta/\varepsilon)^{O(1/\varepsilon^2)} \operatorname{polylog}(n)$ queries per invocation, while Yoshida et al. [SIAM J. Comput.'12] estimate the maximum matching size within additive error $\varepsilon n$ using $\Delta^{O(1/\varepsilon^2)}$ queries. Behnezhad, Roghani, and Rubinstein [FOCS'23] proved a $\Delta^{\Omega(1/\varepsilon)}$ lower bound for both tasks, even on bipartite graphs and even when the LCA's matching guarantee is relaxed to additive $\varepsilon n$ error. This leaves a gap between linear and quadratic dependence on $1/\varepsilon$ in the exponent. We close this gap on bipartite graphs. We give an LCA that answers each mate query with $\Delta^{O(1/\varepsilon)}$ queries for a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximate matching, and an estimator for the maximum matching size within $\varepsilon n$ using $\Delta^{O(1/\varepsilon)}$ queries. On general graphs, the same algorithm gives a half-integral fractional matching and estimates the maximum fractional matching size. Our approach runs $O(\varepsilon^{-1}\log\Delta)$ rounds of a deterministic local optimization method in which vertices propose to neighbors and update prices according to incoming loads. We design its updates to admit exact recursive sampling with constant expected branching, obtaining the improved randomized bound without exploring full dependency neighborhoods. To our knowledge, this is the first LCA construction based on exact recursive sampling of the iterates of a deterministic continuous optimization method. We expect this approach to have applications beyond matching.

papers.title: Efficient Stable Word-RAM Simulation by Population Protocols
papers.abstract: Population protocols model computation by indistinguishable agents interacting in uniformly random pairs, with unary inputs and outputs encoded by state counts. Efficiency requires polylogarithmically many states and polylogarithmic stabilisation time, measured as interactions divided by population size $n$. Stability requires eventual stabilisation to the correct output with probability $1$; silence requires that no agent changes state after stabilisation. Fast stable leader election and majority in leaderless populations require growing state spaces. Despite progress on individual problems, the general computational power of efficient stable protocols remains largely unexplored. We show that it extends beyond semilinear predicates, which characterise constant-state stable computation. We give an efficient, stable, and silent simulation of every $\mathcal{P}$-program: a word-RAM program with running time and number of registers polynomial in $w=\Theta(\log n)$. Stabilisation takes polylogarithmic time both in expectation and with high probability. The framework supports general word-oriented computations, including multiple outputs. The construction extends MC$+$ protocols, fast Monte Carlo protocols whose failures are eventually detected as anomalies, and the system of weights. MC$+$ majority comparisons against the weights convert unary inputs into binary registers, with one agent per bit. MC$+$ operations on individual bits emulate RAM instructions, after which outputs are converted back to unary. A detected anomaly triggers a new universal rank-based backup that stabilises correctly and silently. These results open a systematic study of computational power and resource trade-offs, including extensions to external or spatial data.

papers.title: Sublinear Approximations for Spanning Tree Congestion
papers.abstract: The spanning tree congestion of a connected graph \(G\) is the minimum, over all spanning trees \(T\) of \(G\), of the maximum number of edges of \(G\) crossing a cut induced by deleting an edge of \(T\). In the spanning tree congestion problem we are asked to compute a spanning tree with minimum congestion. We describe two sublinear-ratio approximation algorithms for the spanning tree congestion problem (STC): a simple $\Ot(n^{8/9})$-approximation, and a more involved $\Ot(n^{2/3})$-approximation, where the notation $\Ot$ hides factors polynomial in $\log n$.. Until now, no algorithm with sublinear ratio was known. We also prove that for any fixed $0<\varepsilon<1$, approximation of the spanning tree congestion within $2-\varepsilon$ is NP-hard. This improves the previous best known lower bound $6/5$.

papers.title: Consistent Submodular Maximization with Full Foresight
papers.abstract: Online algorithms with bounded recourse face three intertwined obstacles: uncertainty about the future, computational limits, and a limited budget for changes. We ask a fundamental question that separates consistency from the other two: what does solution stability cost when the entire future is known and computation is unlimited? We answer this question for monotone submodular maximization, where an algorithm must maintain a solution of at most $k$ arrived elements, with a constant number of changes per step. We determine the optimal approximation thresholds: $3/4$ for deterministic algorithms and $\xi^\star \approx 0.7942$ for randomized algorithms. For every $\varepsilon>0$, we get within $\varepsilon$ of these thresholds with worst-case recourse polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$, independent of $k$ and the stream length. We prove matching impossibility results even for coverage functions. We attain the sharp bounds by optimally balancing two opposing forces: preparing for future arrivals and protecting the current solution. For randomized algorithms, we use addition robustness against prefixes of the known future, which we analyze tightly via an interval-selection problem. For deterministic algorithms, we introduce certificates, paths in a fractional relaxation that maintain high value, which we round into an update schedule.

papers.title: A Dichotomy for Terminal Cyclability
papers.abstract: Given an undirected graph $G$ and a set $R \subseteq V(G)$ of terminals, Terminal Cyclability asks whether $G$ contains a simple cycle visiting every vertex of $R$. We establish a complexity dichotomy for this problem on red-minor-closed classes of annotated graphs. In particular, we show that Terminal Cyclability is polynomial-time solvable on every such class excluding any annotated planar graph. The problem is NP-complete whenever the class contains all annotated planar graphs. More precisely, we give an $|G|^{2^{\mathbf{poly}(b)}}$-time algorithm, where $b$ is the bidimensionality of $(G,R)$. Our main technical contribution is the introduction of a weak irrelevant vertex rule. Rather than removing irrelevant vertices until the treewidth becomes constant, we only remove irrelevant vertices until the treewidth is logarithmic in the graph size. Such a weakening is necessary as a parameter-only treewidth threshold for an irrelevant vertex rule in this setting is known to be impossible to realise. Combined with a single-exponential algorithm for Terminal Cyclability parameterized by treewidth, this yields the polynomial-time algorithm for our dichotomy.
